title: What Is a Process?
summary: The process abstraction turns one physical CPU into the illusion of many — a running program's memory, registers, and open files packaged into a single unit the OS can pause, resume, and juggle among many others.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "The Abstraction: The Process"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: The Process API: fork() and exec()
summary: Unix's separation of "create a copy of me" (fork) from "replace my memory with a different program" (exec) — a genuinely strange two-step design whose strangeness is exactly what makes shells and pipes possible.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Interlude: Process API"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: Process States and Context Switching
summary: A process is always in exactly one of a handful of states — running, ready, or blocked — and the mechanism that lets the OS save one process's CPU state and load another's is the context switch, the machinery limited direct execution is built on.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Mechanism: Limited Direct Execution"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: CPU Scheduling: Goals and Metrics
summary: Before comparing scheduling policies, fixing what "good" even means — turnaround time, response time, and throughput often trade off against each other, so no single policy wins on every metric at once.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Scheduling: Introduction"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: FCFS, SJF, and the Convoy Effect
summary: First-come-first-served is trivially fair but lets one long job block every short job behind it — the convoy effect — while shortest-job-first fixes average turnaround time provably, at the cost of needing to know the future.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Scheduling: Introduction"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: Round-Robin and Time-Slicing
summary: Giving every job a small, fixed time slice and cycling through them in turn — excellent for response time, worse for turnaround time than SJF, and the first policy in this discipline that doesn't need to predict the future.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Scheduling: Introduction"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: Priority Scheduling and Starvation
summary: Letting some jobs jump the queue solves the problem of urgent work waiting behind trivial work, but opens a new one — a low-priority job can wait forever if higher-priority work never stops arriving.

references.label: UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: Multi-Level Feedback Queue Scheduling
summary: The scheduler real operating systems actually approximate: multiple priority queues, jobs demoted for using too much CPU and promoted periodically to prevent starvation — learning a job's behavior from its recent history instead of asking it up front.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: Threads and the Shared Address Space
summary: A thread is a separately schedulable stream of execution that shares its process's address space with its sibling threads — the exact systems-level mechanics that the shared-state concurrency model, introduced conceptually elsewhere, is actually built from.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Concurrency: An Introduction"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: The Critical Section Problem and Mutual Exclusion
summary: The formal statement of the race-condition hazard already met as a mental model: a critical section is any code touching shared state, and mutual exclusion is the guarantee that at most one thread is inside it at a time.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Concurrency: An Introduction"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: Locks and Atomic Hardware Primitives
summary: A lock only works if acquiring it is itself immune to the same race condition it prevents — which is why real locks are built on hardware-provided atomic instructions like test-and-set and compare-and-swap, not on ordinary load/store.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Locks"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: Condition Variables
summary: A lock alone can't let a thread wait for some condition to become true without busy-spinning — a condition variable adds exactly that: a queue a thread can sleep on, and a signal another thread sends when the wait is over.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Condition Variables"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: Semaphores
summary: A single integer counter with two atomic operations, wait and signal, general enough to implement a lock, a condition variable's signaling, or a bound on how many threads may proceed at once — Dijkstra's one primitive that does the job of several.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Semaphores"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: Deadlock: Conditions and Detection
summary: Locks and semaphores solve races but open a new failure mode: threads waiting on each other in a cycle, forever — deadlock, detectable by building a resource-allocation graph and running the exact same cycle-detection algorithm already covered for graphs in general.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Concurrency Bugs"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: Address Spaces and Memory Virtualization
summary: Every process sees its own private, contiguous address space starting at address zero — an illusion the OS maintains on top of one shared physical RAM, and the reason a bug in one program's pointers can't corrupt another program's memory.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Address Spaces"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: Address Translation: Base and Bound
summary: The simplest possible hardware support for virtualized memory: one register holding where a process's memory starts, another holding how big it is — every address a program uses gets relocated and checked against the bound automatically.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Mechanism: Address Translation"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: Segmentation and Free-Space Management
summary: Splitting an address space into independently relocated segments (code, stack, heap) avoids wasting memory on the unused gap between a small heap and a small stack — at the cost of external fragmentation, the same free-space-management problem a general-purpose allocator faces.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Segmentation"
Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Free-Space Management"

title: Paging and Page Tables
summary: Instead of a few large, variable-sized segments, chop memory into many small, fixed-size pages — eliminating external fragmentation entirely, at the cost of needing a page table to record where every single page actually lives in physical memory.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Paging: Introduction"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: The Translation Lookaside Buffer
summary: Looking up a page table entry in memory on every single memory access would make paging catastrophically slow — the TLB is a small, fully associative hardware cache of recent translations, applying the same caching idea already covered for data, now to address translation itself.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs)"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: Page Replacement Policies
summary: When physical memory is full and a new page must be brought in, something has to be evicted — FIFO, optimal, and LRU are three different answers to "which page," compared on the exact same reference string to see how many page faults each one actually causes.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Beyond Physical Memory: Policies"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: Demand Paging and Thrashing
summary: Loading pages only when they're actually touched lets a process run with less physical memory than its full address space needs — until too many processes compete for too little memory and the system spends more time paging than computing, a collapse called thrashing.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Complete Virtual Memory Systems"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming

title: Files, Directories, and Inodes
summary: A file system's real job is turning a flat array of disk blocks into named, hierarchical files — an inode holds one file's metadata and the block pointers that locate its data, while a directory is just a special file mapping names to inode numbers.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Files and Directories"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: File System Implementation and Journaling
summary: A crash in the middle of a multi-block update (a new inode, a new data block, an updated bitmap) can leave a file system's on-disk structures inconsistent — journaling fixes this by writing the intended changes to a log first, making the whole update recoverable as a single atomic step.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "File System Implementation"
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: Capstone: Tracing a Process from fork() to Page Fault to Disk
summary: Every mechanism in this discipline working together on one concrete timeline: a shell forks and execs a program, the scheduler picks it, it touches a page that isn't resident yet, and the resulting page fault ends in a real disk read through the file system.

references.label: Arpaci-Dusseau — Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, "Complete Virtual Memory Systems"
UC Berkeley CS162 — Operating Systems and Systems Programming
